AI Agents Can Be Responsible. They Can Never Be Accountable. Here's the Distinction That Decides Who Survives the Next Two Years.

Three separate conversations this week landed on the same point from three different angles: the real risk isn't what an agent can do, it's who owns the decision when it does something nobody expected. That's not a coincidence — it's exactly the gap regulators in Singapore, Brussels and Washington have spent 2026 writing into law.

LW
Lisa Warren
Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI · September 28, 2026

Picture a portfolio review. Overnight, an AI agent flagged a cost anomaly, drafted the escalation note, updated the risk register, and notified stakeholders — all before anyone arrived in the room. Someone finally asks the obvious question: "who owns this risk?" Silence. Not because nobody is smart enough to answer. Because nobody assigned the answer before the agent started acting.

That scenario is playing out in enterprises right now, and it's the exact reason a handful of senior leaders keep independently landing on the same insight: the hard part of agentic AI was never capability. It's ownership.

Key Takeaways

  • The RACI rule most deployments break: an AI agent can hold Responsible, Consulted or Informed roles. It can never hold Accountable. That seat stays with a named human, full stop.
  • It's already law, not just best practice: Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (22 January 2026) — the world's first governance framework built specifically for autonomous agents — makes "meaningful human accountability" one of its four core pillars, and states plainly that organisations remain legally accountable for their agents' actions regardless of whether they follow the voluntary framework.
  • The EU has done the same thing through a different door: the EU AI Act's Article 14 human-oversight duty falls on the organisation deploying the system — the "relying party" — not on the AI vendor or the model itself.
  • The identity gap is the quiet emergency: the US NIST/NCCoE AI Agent Standards Initiative, launched February 2026, warns that most enterprises still treat agents as generic service accounts with no dedicated identity, authorization or accountability trail — meaning many organisations literally cannot say which agent, acting under whose authority, took a given action.
  • 92% of CIOs have already been asked to defend an AI outcome they could not fully explain, according to a Dataiku/Harris Poll survey.
  • The fix isn't more caution about deploying agents. It's assigning ownership by decision stage — build, permissions, policy, monitoring, escalation — before deployment, not after an incident forces you to reconstruct who was supposed to be watching.

The scenario playing out in boardrooms right now

An AI agent works overnight inside a portfolio management system. It spots a cost anomaly, drafts an escalation note, updates the risk register, and notifies the relevant stakeholders — all without a human in the loop. By the time the team sits down for the morning review, the paperwork is already done and largely correct. Then someone asks who owns the underlying risk the agent just surfaced, and the room goes quiet. Nobody updated the governance model when the agent was switched on, so nobody was ever assigned that answer.

This is not a rare edge case. It's the default outcome of deploying agentic AI into a governance structure built for software that only ever did what it was told, when it was told. The moment a system starts acting on its own initiative, the old assumption — that a human somewhere in the chain was always the one who pressed "go" — quietly stops being true, and almost nobody updates the org chart to reflect it.

Why agents can never hold the "A" in RACI

RACI — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — has been the standard way of assigning ownership on a project for decades. Applied to agentic AI, the framework still works, with one rule that most current deployments are quietly breaking: an agent can be the one who does the work (Responsible), the one whose input shapes it (Consulted), or the one kept aware of it (Informed). It can never be the one who is ultimately answerable for the outcome. That seat has to stay with a named human, and — critically — that human's accountability increases, not decreases, the more autonomy the agent is given.

Most organizations deploying agents today haven't updated their governance model to reflect this at all. They've simply pointed an existing team at an agent and assumed accountability would sort itself out by default. It doesn't. It just goes unassigned until an incident forces the question — which is precisely why 92% of CIOs surveyed by Dataiku and Harris Poll say they've already been asked to defend an AI decision they couldn't fully explain. That's not a technology gap. It's a named-owner gap.

"An agent can act. It can never be accountable. The moment you forget that distinction is the moment 'who approved this' becomes a question nobody in the room can answer."

— Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

The regulators are already writing this into law

This isn't a theoretical governance nicety anymore. On 22 January 2026, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority launched the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI — the world's first governance framework built specifically for AI agents capable of autonomous planning, reasoning and action. Compliance is voluntary. Legal accountability is not: the framework states explicitly that organisations remain legally accountable for their agents' behaviour and actions regardless of whether they choose to follow it. Its four pillars are risk-bounding, meaningful human accountability, technical controls, and end-user responsibility — and "meaningful human accountability" means defining, in advance, the specific checkpoints at which a human has to approve an action before the agent can take it.

The EU AI Act reaches the same destination through a different route. Article 14's human-oversight obligation, and Article 15's accuracy and robustness requirements, apply to autonomous agents operating in high-risk domains — and the duty to satisfy them falls on the "relying party," meaning the organisation deploying the system, not the vendor who built the underlying model.

Meanwhile, in the US, the NIST Center for AI Standards and Innovation's AI Agent Standards Initiative, launched in February 2026, is tackling the problem from the identity layer up. Its own framing is blunt: agents are commonly treated as generic service accounts, without the dedicated identity, authorization or accountability controls that would let an organisation actually trace which agent, acting under whose authority, took a given action. Singapore's framework makes the same point from the opposite direction — as agents grow more autonomous, identity management has to extend to them individually, precisely so someone can always answer who holds accountability for that specific agent's behaviour.

Ownership by decision stage, not by department

The organisations getting this right aren't assigning agent ownership by software category — "IT owns the tool, so IT owns the outcome." They're assigning it by decision lifecycle stage, because an autonomous decision is rarely produced by one team acting alone. It's what one governance framework aptly calls a decision supply chain: someone owns the technical build and orchestration layer, someone owns permission design and access controls, someone owns the policy and regulatory boundaries the agent has to operate inside, someone owns ongoing monitoring and drift detection, and — separately from all of that — someone is the named escalation point who can approve or override the agent's action when it hits a boundary.

That last role is the one most organisations skip, because it's the least exciting item on the list. It's also the one that determines whether "who approved this" has an answer on the day it actually matters. A tested shutdown path only counts as tested if someone other than the team that built the agent verified it works — the people who designed the permissions are the worst-placed people to find the gaps in them.

What to put in place before your next agent goes live

  • Name a human Accountable owner for every agent, individually, before it goes into production — not a team, not "the AI committee," one person whose name is on the outcome.
  • Give every agent its own identity in your systems, not a shared service account, so every action it takes traces back to a specific authorization. This is the exact gap NIST's Agent Standards Initiative was created to close.
  • Map ownership to decision stage, not to whichever team happened to build the tool — build and orchestration, permissions and access, policy and regulatory boundaries, monitoring and drift detection, and escalation authority are five different jobs, and they rarely belong to the same person.
  • Define the human-approval checkpoints in advance, the way Singapore's framework requires — decide before deployment which actions an agent can take alone and which ones require a person to say yes first, rather than discovering the boundary during an incident.
  • Have someone outside the build team test the shutdown path. A kill-switch verified only by the people who designed it is a kill-switch nobody has actually tested.

Lisa Warren: the reframe

"Missing authority doesn't announce itself. There's no breach, no incident — just an agent quietly making calls nobody signed off on, for months, until someone finally asks who approved this, and the room goes quiet."

— Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

The question every board should be asking now

Not "what can our agents do." Not even "are our agents safe." The question that actually protects an organisation is narrower and more uncomfortable: for every agent currently live, can you name the specific human who is accountable if it does something nobody expected — and would that person agree, right now, that they know they hold that role? If the honest answer is silence, that's not a technology gap. Singapore, the EU and the US have all just spent the first months of 2026 confirming, in three different legal systems, that it's the only gap that actually matters.

Move from headlines to implementation

If you can't currently name the accountable human owner for every AI agent live in your organisation, that's the first thing worth fixing — before the next feature, not after the next incident.
